transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I'm here because I've been feeling completely exhausted and drained all the time, and it has been going on for about a year and a half now. On top of the physical fatigue, I'm constantly struggling with this uncontrollable worry that I just can't seem to turn off.

Regarding the feeling of being drained and the constant worry, have you experienced these symptoms almost every single day for the past 18 months, or have there been periods where you felt completely like yourself?

Yes, it has been pretty much every single day for the past year and a half. I haven't had any real breaks or periods where I felt like my normal self at all during this time. It just feels like a constant, daily struggle of being completely drained and worried.
During this time, have you lost interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, or do you feel a persistent sense of sadness or hopelessness?

No, I wouldn't say I feel hopeless or have lost interest in things, it's just that I'm too exhausted to do them. My main struggles are really this constant, uncontrollable worry, feeling completely drained, and being physically tense and easily irritated all the time.
Do you find that your constant worry makes it difficult for you to fall asleep, stay asleep, or feel rested when you wake up in the morning?
I'm not really sure if I have trouble actually falling or staying asleep. But no matter what, I always wake up feeling completely exhausted and unrefreshed, even after getting rest.
Do you notice that you experience muscle tension, such as tightness in your shoulders or neck, or do you find yourself feeling restless and unable to sit still for long periods?
Yes, my body constantly feels incredibly stiff and tense, as if I just can't relax my muscles. I also frequently feel wound up like a spring, which makes it really hard to sit still or stay calm.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports a 1.5-year history of constant, uncontrollable worry, physical tension, irritability, and feeling 'wound up,' which strongly supports Generalized Anxiety Disorder. The patient explicitly denied feelings of hopelessness or loss of interest (anhedonia), which makes Persistent Depressive Disorder significantly less likely. Therefore, I have removed Persistent Depressive Disorder from the candidates.
